specAnchors.text: understand reasons for the trend in ionisation energy down Groups 1 and 2

primer.text: Groups 1 and 2 are electron donors: one or two outer electrons, willingly surrendered. This note tracks the first and second ionisation energies down both groups and explains why bigger atoms let go more easily, even though their nuclei hold more protons than their neighbours above.

modules.title: Outer electrons and the ionisation climb
modules.opening: Groups 1 and 2 exist to donate: one or two electrons in the outermost principal quantum shell, surrendered to form +1 or +2 ions. This lesson sets the donation in motion, names the agents, and connects the electron handover to oxidation numbers.
keyPoints: Group 1 atoms carry one electron and Group 2 atoms two, both sitting in the outermost principal quantum shell.
Donating those electrons forms ionic compounds with +1 or +2 cations.
A species that donates electrons acts as a reducing agent.
The donating metal is itself oxidised, climbing its oxidation number.
Both groups grow more reactive as the descent proceeds.

low.restatement: The outer shell holds the giveaway electrons; losing one (Group 1) or two (Group 2) leaves a stable cation, and the metal pays for the partner's reduction by being oxidised itself.
low.analogy: Two donation boxes at the door: the Group 1 box takes single coins, the Group 2 box takes pairs - and the donor's wallet (oxidation number) lightens by the same count.
low.examPointer: Link the phrases in one chain: donates electrons, therefore reducing agent, therefore oxidised itself - dropping a link costs the mark.

medium.restatement: Ionisation removes electrons from the outermost principal quantum shell; the resulting noble-gas-like cation is stabilised in ionic compounds, and the metal's reducing-agent role is exactly the electron-donation half of the redox pair.
medium.analogy: A courier handing over parcels: the courier (metal) ends each delivery lighter (oxidised) while the recipient (non-metal partner) is loaded (reduced).
medium.examPointer: For 'why are these metals reducing agents' items, answer through electron donation - never through reactivity alone.

modules.title: Reading the ionisation energy graph
modules.opening: The graph shows both first and second ionisation energies sinking down Group 2 - and the same pattern runs through Group 1. This lesson weighs the contest between rising nuclear charge and the shielding-plus-distance pair that outvotes it.
keyPoints: The first ionisation energy removes the first outer electron; the second removes the next.
Both first and second ionisation energies decrease going down Group 2.
Group 1 shows the same downward trend in its first ionisation energy.
Nuclear charge increases down the group as protons accumulate.
Increased shielding and larger nucleus-to-electron distance outweigh the extra protons.

low.restatement: Down the group each new shell pushes the outer electrons further out and wraps them in more shielding, so removal gets cheaper despite the growing nucleus.
low.analogy: A king's herald shouting across a growing courtyard: more guards (shells) stand between the throne (nucleus) and the gate (outer electron), and every extra metre weakens the royal voice.
low.examPointer: Name BOTH outweighing factors - increased shielding AND larger distance - a single-factor answer scores half.

medium.restatement: Ionisation energy tracks the net attraction on the outermost electrons; added core shells raise shielding while radius growth lowers Coulomb attraction, together beating the proton-driven charge rise and tipping both IE1 and IE2 downward.
medium.analogy: Paying rent through an intermediary chain: each new middleman (shell) takes a cut (shields), and the longer corridor (distance) weakens the landlord's grip more than his bigger vault (more protons) compensates.
medium.examPointer: Tie the graph's two curves together: the same physics drives both ionisation energies, so quoting one curve's explanation covers both.

glossary.definition: The energy that removes an atom's first outer electron in the gas phase.
The energy that removes the second outer electron once the first has gone.
The reduction of nuclear pull on outer electrons caused by intervening inner shells.
